notes.meaning: Antiochus makes treaties and alliances with others, but he uses these promises to trick them. Even though he starts with only a small group of followers, he quickly gains power through cunning moves. His rise shows how dangerous false peace can be.

During a time when people feel safe, he moves unexpectedly into the richest areas. He gives away stolen wealth and plunder to win over loyal followers, doing far more than his ancestors ever did. He also plots against key fortresses, but his plans last only as long as God allows.

He gathers courage and leads a massive army against the king of the South, who rules Egypt. The Egyptian king comes out to fight with a huge, powerful army of his own. Yet Egypt fails to win because of secret plots worked out behind the scenes.

The king of Egypt is betrayed by his own close advisers and table companions. Because of their secret treachery, his army is scattered and overwhelmed like a flood. Many of his soldiers fall dead on the battlefield.

The two rival kings sit together at the same meal and speak smooth lies to one another. Each pretends to want peace while secretly planning to destroy the other. None of their schemes work out, because God has already set the exact time for the end.

Antiochus heads back home toward Syria carrying immense plunder taken from Egypt. Along the way, his anger turns against God's people and the holy covenant. He attacks Jerusalem and plunders the temple before returning to his own country.
At the time God permits, Antiochus invades Egypt a second time. He hopes for another easy victory over the south. This time, however, things do not turn out the way they did before.

Roman warships arrive from the west and their envoys firmly order him to retreat. Humiliated and fearful of Rome's power, he backs down and marches away in shame. He vents his burning anger on the Jews in Jerusalem, showing special favor to those who turn their backs on God's law.

His soldiers march into Jerusalem and defile the temple, which served as a sacred stronghold. They put an end to the daily sacrifices offered to the Lord. In their place, they set up an idol to Zeus on the altar, an act called the abomination of desolation.

Antiochus uses flattering words and promises of reward to lead unfaithful Jews completely away from God. In contrast, those who truly love and know their God stand strong against his pressure. They refuse to give up their faith and take bold action to resist him.

Faithful teachers with spiritual wisdom instruct the people and keep many from giving up the truth. Yet these loyal believers pay a terrible price for standing firm. For a period of time, they are cut down by swords, burned, captured, and robbed of their belongings.

When the faithful suffer, God gives them a little relief through the brave revolt of the Maccabees. This small help brings encouragement, but it does not end all their troubles. Soon, many insincere people join their movement only because it is winning, not out of true devotion to God.

Even some of the wisest spiritual leaders are allowed to fall under cruel persecution. God uses these painful trials like fire to test, refine, and cleanse his people. This season of suffering will not last forever, because God has already set the exact time for it to end.

This ruler acts completely according to his own arrogant will, exalting himself above every god. He utters shocking, boastful words against the one true God who rules heaven and earth. He enjoys success for a season, but only until God's decreed punishment is finished.

differ.view: This ruler was Antiochus Epiphanes, who served as a vivid prophetic picture of the future Antichrist.
The prophecy shifts here from Antiochus to describe the long rise and power of the Roman Empire.
The text leaps across the centuries to describe the final end-time Antichrist.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The description continues to picture Antiochus IV, portraying his legendary pride in heightened poetic language.

notes.meaning: He turns away from the traditional gods worshipped by his ancestors. He shows no regard for the deity cherished by women or for any other god. In his supreme pride, he considers himself greater than everything else.

Instead of old faiths, he honors a god of fortresses and raw armed power. He spends huge amounts of gold, silver, and precious jewels to build up his war machine. For him, military might and worldly strength become the real object of worship.

Relying on this devotion to military force, he attacks and captures the strongest fortified cities. He showers great honor and authority on those who bend the knee to him. He rewards his loyal followers by setting them up as rulers and selling off lands for profit.

At the time of the end, the king of the South strikes out against him in battle. The king of the North answers by charging back like a violent storm with chariots, horsemen, and many ships. His forces sweep through many lands, overflowing them like a raging river.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because Antiochus never fought a campaign like this at the end of his life, these verses likely express an idealized prophetic picture rather than recorded history.

notes.meaning: He marches his invading army into the beautiful land of Israel, and many surrounding regions fall before him. Even so, the neighboring border lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon escape his power. God sets clear boundaries on what the conqueror is able to touch.

He reaches out his conquering hand to take over nation after nation. Even mighty Egypt cannot withstand his advance or escape his grasp. His widespread success makes him appear completely unstoppable.

He gains control over the massive wealth of Egypt, carrying off its gold, silver, and finest treasures. The peoples of Libya and Cush submit to him and march under his command. His greed for wealth matches his thirst for world conquest.

While celebrating his victories, alarming reports from the east and north deeply shake him. He flies into a blind rage and sets out with great fury to wipe out his enemies. He is determined to destroy and completely crush all who stand in his way.

He sets up his grand royal tents between the Mediterranean Sea and Mount Zion, God's holy mountain. Yet right at the height of his pride, he meets a sudden and total end. When God brings his final judgment, no human ally can do anything to rescue him.
